Content.Strong: Early-Z is not an absolute promise

Chapter.Content: We discussed early versus late depth in Pass 1.
The fragment pipeline may contain operations that constrain early testing, such as explicit depth writes or certain fragment-side effects.
Vulkan’s fragment pipeline defines depth/stencil testing as part of per-fragment operations and exposes explicit early/late fragment-test execution stages. docs.vulkan.org
Modern implementations also use hierarchical rejection before individual sample tests.
So “early-Z” should be understood as a family of implementations that avoid fragment work when visibility can be proven, not one mandatory little hardware block.

Content.Strong: Mesh shaders change the pre-rasterization model

Chapter.Content: The classic path is:
Chapter.Code: vertex/index buffer ↓ fixed-function vertex fetch ↓ primitive assembly ↓ vertex shader ↓ optional tessellation/geometry stages ↓ rasterizer
Chapter.Content: Mesh shaders replace much of this front end with workgroup-programmable geometry generation.
Conceptually:
Chapter.Code: workgroup reads meshlet data performs culling generates vertices generates primitive indices ↓ rasterizer
Chapter.Content: Khronos describes VK_EXT_mesh_shader as a compute-like programmable mechanism that can replace the traditional pre-rasterization vertex/primitive pipeline, with mesh shaders producing vertices and primitives directly for rasterization. docs.vulkan.org
Mesh shaders become much easier to understand if you first understand meshlets.
Instead of one giant indexed mesh:
Chapter.Code: 500,000 triangles
Chapter.Content: partition it into small clusters, for example:
Chapter.Code: meshlet: ≤ 64 vertices ≤ 126 triangles bounding sphere normal cone material
Chapter.Content: Now each cluster becomes a convenient unit for:
Chapter.Code: frustum culling cone/backface culling LOD parallel processing
Chapter.Content: A mesh shader workgroup can process one meshlet.
It loads its compact local vertex/index data, rejects the entire cluster if invisible, and otherwise emits the required vertices and primitives.
This creates much finer control over geometry processing than the traditional “feed vertices one by one through fixed assembly” model.
Task shaders are an optional stage before mesh shaders.
Their mental model is:
Chapter.Code: task workgroup ↓ coarse analysis / culling / LOD ↓ decide how many mesh workgroups exist ↓ emit payload ↓ mesh shader workgroups
Chapter.Content: A task shader might inspect a collection of meshlets and decide:
Chapter.Code: meshlets 0–11 invisible → launch nothing meshlet 12 visible → launch one mesh group meshlet 13 high detail → launch several groups
Chapter.Content: Current Khronos documentation emphasizes exactly this role: task shaders can perform coarse culling and dynamically emit mesh shader groups via a workgroup-level payload. docs.vulkan.org
Important: mesh shaders are not automatically faster.
The extension documentation itself warns that their flexibility can incur platform-dependent cost and that optimized traditional pipelines may remain faster for some workloads. docs.vulkan.org
That is the right engineering attitude.

Content.Strong: A black frame is not one bug

Chapter.Content: Suppose the application window appears and nothing renders.
“Graphics are broken” is too vague to be useful.
The frame is a dependency chain:
A systematic debugger asks:
Do not randomly edit shaders.
Bisect the rendering machine.
Use this exact order because each stage removes huge classes of hypotheses.

ListItem.Content: Prove the frame exists at all. Clear the target to violent magenta. If magenta never reaches the screen, geometry and shaders are irrelevant; inspect acquire/record/submit/present and render-target routing. In Kairo, that means following VulkanRendererRuntime::DrawFrame: wait/retire → acquire → record → submit → present.

Prove the correct render target is being written. Kairo renders the 3D scene into VulkanViewportTarget, then later presents UI to the swapchain. A valid swapchain does not prove the offscreen viewport pass is correct.
Remove geometry complexity. Draw one hard-coded triangle with no index buffer, no material, no textures, no lighting, no skinning.
Remove depth and culling. Disable depth and face culling. If the triangle appears, reintroduce those independently.
Replace the fragment shader with constant output. outColor = vec4(1,0,1,1);. If it now appears, rasterization works and the failure is downstream of interpolation/material shading.
Trace one vertex numerically. Record object, world, view, clip and NDC coordinates. Verify finite , clip inequalities and expected screen position.
Check vertex layout contracts. Buffer stride, offsets, formats and shader locations must describe the same bytes.
Check draw ranges. Index count, index type, bound offsets, vertex offsets and actual buffer sizes.
Check attachment compatibility and writes. Pipeline render-pass compatibility, color write masks, blend state, depth state and final image layouts.
Only then inspect sophisticated systems. Descriptor contents, material textures, normal maps, shadow passes, HDR exposure and render-graph synchronization.

Chapter.Content: That is our one deliberate list for the pass because it is meant to become an actual debugging procedure.

Chapter.Content: Now we can map every significant CPU operation to GPU machinery.
This is Part 1900.
And it is the point of the entire phase.
The GPU pipeline is no longer a diagram you memorize.
It is a hardware-parallel implementation of mechanisms you could reconstruct yourself.

Content.Strong: One subtle Kairo issue worth understanding: transparent object IDs

Chapter.Content: Your viewport has two color outputs:
Chapter.Code: HDR color object ID
Chapter.Content: The color attachment can blend.
The object-ID attachment does not use blending.
So a transparent fragment that passes depth testing can write an object ID even though its visible color may only contribute partially.
Because transparent depth writes are disabled, the relationship among:
Chapter.Code: visible composited surface object picking identity draw order
Chapter.Content: is not necessarily trivial.
This is not automatically wrong.
For an editor, picking the nearest submitted transparent object may be desired.
But once transparent overlap becomes complex, picking semantics must be explicitly defined.
Questions arise such as:
Chapter.Code: Should nearly invisible glass be pickable? Should alpha < 0.05 count? Should masked holes write IDs? Should transparent object picking use a separate pass?
Chapter.Content: That is a real engine-design issue hidden behind what looks like a simple second attachment.

Content.Strong: Another Kairo issue: transparent sort key is object-origin distance

Chapter.Content: Current sorting uses distance squared from camera to model translation.
That avoids square roots because:
for nonnegative distances.
Good.
But it is not equivalent to true per-fragment ordering.
Consider a wall-sized transparent quad whose origin lies far away but which extends in front of another object’s center.
The sort key cannot capture that geometry.
Production renderers therefore combine strategies such as:

Content.Strong: How the pipeline state interacts rather than existing independently

Chapter.Content: A common weak understanding is to learn:
Chapter.Code: culling depth blending MSAA stencil
Chapter.Content: as separate checkboxes.
They interact.
Consider foliage.
If you use alpha blending:
Chapter.Code: backface culling maybe disabled depth testing enabled depth writes often disabled back-to-front ordering needed overdraw high early-Z usefulness reduced
Chapter.Content: If you instead use cutout alpha:
Chapter.Code: depth writes can remain enabled sorting becomes easier but discard introduces aliasing
Chapter.Content: If you add MSAA + alpha-to-coverage:
Chapter.Code: coverage becomes sample-based depth can remain per-sample cutout edges become smoother bandwidth rises
Chapter.Content: This is the kind of system-level reasoning you need to choose techniques rather than name them.
A typical opaque pass wants something close to:
Chapter.Code: backface culling ON depth test ON depth write ON blend OFF front-to-back-ish sort MSAA optional stencil technique-dependent
Chapter.Content: because opaque surfaces obey a simple visibility invariant:
Depth is extraordinarily effective for this case.
Traditional sorted transparency looks more like:
Chapter.Code: depth test ON depth write OFF blend ON back-to-front sorting culling material-dependent
Chapter.Content: because a transparent surface does not erase all radiance behind it.
This destroys many of the nice ordering freedoms opaque rendering has.
That is why transparent rendering is disproportionately difficult relative to the simple blend equation.
Suppose culling changes per material.
You could compile:
Chapter.Code: opaque_cull_back opaque_two_sided transparent_cull_back transparent_two_sided ...
Chapter.Content: or make cull mode dynamic when supported.
Dynamic state reduces pipeline count.
But there is no universal rule that “more dynamic state is better.”
Hardware/driver implementation, pipeline compilation, command recording and state-change frequency all matter.

Content.Strong: Pipeline cache versus engine-level PSO cache

Chapter.Content: Do not confuse two caches.
An engine PSO cache might map:
Chapter.Code: PipelineKey → VkPipeline
Chapter.Content: where PipelineKey includes:
Chapter.Code: shader variant blend mode depth mode cull mode vertex layout render target formats
Chapter.Content: This avoids creating duplicate Vulkan pipelines.
A Vulkan VkPipelineCache, meanwhile, lets the driver reuse internal compilation artifacts during pipeline creation.
They solve different layers:
A mature renderer often has both.
Suppose normal mapping is optional.
Approach A:
Chapter.Code: if (material.hasNormalMap) ApplyNormalMap();
Chapter.Content: One shader.
Potential divergence and unnecessary resources.
Approach B:
Chapter.Code: NORMAL_MAP=0 shader NORMAL_MAP=1 shader
Chapter.Content: No runtime branch, but another permutation dimension.
If there are 20 such features, compiling every combination becomes impossible.
A production strategy often categorizes features:
Chapter.Code:
large structural feature → permutation
small cheap coherent choice → runtime uniform branch
material specialization known at pipeline creation → specialization constant
entirely separate rendering technique → separate pass/shader family
Chapter.Content: This is shader architecture, not merely shader syntax.

Chapter.Content: That changes ownership and debugging.
Your old debugging question:

BlockQuote.Content: “Did CPU code call DrawIndexed for object 518?”

Chapter.Content: becomes:

BlockQuote.Content: “Did compute classify instance 518 visible, did it survive compaction, did its indirect record get written, did synchronization make that record visible, and did the indirect draw consume it?”

A mature implementation therefore needs debugging buffers, counters and capture tools from the start.
